title: Integrated fidelity, chaos and benchmark hardening manual
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Purpose and scope

This document describes a repeatable, integrated workflow that teams should use to: (1) validate inference fidelity under stress and kernel-scheduling perturbations, (2) harden our benchmarking suite against flakiness introduced by noisy co-tenants and thermal/power events, and (3) produce actionable profiling artifacts suitable for runtime triage and production runbooks. The goal is to produce deterministic reports and remediation recipes used in release signoffs and incident runbooks.

Summary of approach

- Combine orthogonal test axes: fidelity (model output quality), performance (latency/throughput/tail), and stability (resource contention, scheduler perturbation, thermal events).
- Use a staged pipeline: quick unit microbenchmarks -> controlled chaos experiments -> long-running production-sim replicas -> postmortem profiling and remediation.
- Require a benchmark gate: no release to canary without passing the hardening checklist (see "Release gate checklist").

Key definitions and SLOs

- Fidelity SLO: top-1 generation agreement with golden prompt-set >= 98% for model family X (measured by normalized BLEU/ROUGE + Redwood output policy checks).
- Tail latency SLO: P99 for generation under target sequence length <= 1500 tokens must be < 300 ms for dedicated pool class d2-small; P999 < 600 ms for critical routes.
- Cost drift tolerance: per-token cost variance <= 7% across benchmark runs on the same hardware flavor.
- Stability: no sustained GPU memory OOMs, no kernel watchdog resets during a 6-hour production replica run.

Pipeline stages (high level)

1) Microbenchmark sweep (duration: ~30m)
   - Purpose: detect immediate regressions in kernel latencies and basic memory safety.
   - Tasks: run synthetic microbenchmarks that exercise attention, matmul, kv-cache read/write and quantized matmul kernels.
   - Output: kernel latency histogram, occupancy profile, quick pass/fail.

2) Controlled scheduling perturbation (duration: ~1–2h)
   - Purpose: validate scheduler fairness and preemption heuristics.
   - Tasks: inject load on same node (cpu/gpu) with synthetic co-tenants; toggle scheduler knobs (preemptive-slice-ms, slot-max-coalesce).
   - Output: degraded latency curves, fairness metric, recommendation for knob adjustments.

3) Fidelity under stress (duration: ~2–6h)
   - Purpose: ensure model outputs stay within acceptable quality while under load and degraded kernel fidelity (e.g., using lower-precision paths).
   - Tasks: replay golden prompt corpus while intermittently forcing quantized execution paths and ephemeral preemption events.
   - Output: fidelity delta report and failcases list.

4) Production replica soak (duration: 6–24h)
   - Purpose: reveal long-tail and thermal/power-induced flakiness.
   - Tasks: run scaled request mix from production sampling; enable observability (trace, kernel metrics, nvml), record incidents.
   - Output: long-run telemetry, incident log, candidate mitigations.

5) Profiling and triage (duration: variable)
   - Purpose: capture CPU/GPU/kernel traces and synthesize a remediation recipe.
   - Tasks: collect compact traces, annotate with request provenance, run offline causal attribution.
   - Output: triage ticket with recommended kernel or scheduler changes and runbook updates.

Instrumentation checklist

All pipeline runs must include the following signals at minimum:

- Request-level: request_id, route, model_version, input_length, output_length, tokens_generated, client_tier.
- Runtime-level: kernel_id, kernel_duration_us, kernel_queue_delay_us, kernel_backpressure_level, slot_id.
- GPU-level: nvml temperature, power_draw_w, gpu_mem_used_mb, gpu_util_pct.
- Host-level: CPU load, cgroups memory usage, interrupts/sec.
- Observability: trace sample rate, span annotations for preemption events, synthetic failure markers.

Config table (recommended starting knobs)

| Knob | Default | Recommended during tests | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| preemptive_slice_ms | 10 | 5 / 20 (sweep) | Lower values increase preemption frequency; helpful to detect priority inversion. |
| slot_max_coalesce | 4 | 2–8 (sweep) | Controls batch coalescing; affects latency/throughput tradeoff. |
| kv_cache_prefetch | true | true/false (toggle) | Prefetch warmer reduces tail but may increase mem pressure. |
| kernel_hedge_threshold_ms | 200 | 100–400 (sweep) | Hedge slow kernels to alternate implementations. |
| quant_path | int8-fp32-mix | int8 / fp16 / fp32 | Exercise mixed precision paths for fidelity testing. |

How to run (CLI recipes)

1) Kick off microbenchmark sweep\n
shell> ri-bench run --suite microkernel-sweep --node-selector gcp-a2 --duration 30m --out /tmp/bench_run_$(date +%s)

2) Run controlled scheduling perturbation (example script)

shell> ri-chaos inject-scheduler --target-node node-123 --co-tenants 3 --pattern burst:5m/idle:10m --knob preemptive_slice_ms=5,slot_max_coalesce=2 --trace-output s3://redwood-test/chaos/$(date +%F_%T)

3) Fidelity validation run (yaml example)

---
name: fidelity-replay-2026-02
prompts: s3://redwood-golden-corpora/serving-replay/v1
model: rdx-open-1.3
quantization_paths: [int8,fp16]
concurrency: 64
duration: 03:00:00
trace: true
report_output: s3://redwood-results/fidelity/2026-02-01/report.json

Interpreting outputs

- Kernel histograms: look for multimodal distributions; bimodality usually indicates two kernel variants being used or a scheduler boundary.
- Fidelity deltas: group failcases by prompt archetype and by quantization path. If failures cluster on math-heavy prompts -> suspect lower-precision accumulation error.
- Resource trends: monotonic GPU memory creeping over a soak indicates a leak; spikes in nvlink error counters suggest hardware-level issues to escalate.

Runbook excerpt: when P99 regression observed after kernel rollout

1) Immediately set rollback flag for the kernel bundle: ri-runtime rollback-kernel --bundle-id <bundle> --reason "p99_regression"
2) Throttle new canary traffic to 10% and enable shadow-mode for kernel variant A vs B.
3) Capture compact traces for 1 hour (trace-sampler 100%) and run the causal attribution pipeline: ri-proftec analyze --input s3://... --output /tmp/causal_report.json
4) If rollback is not possible, apply short-term mitigations: increase slot_max_coalesce to coalesce small batches (reduces kernel invocations) and toggle kv_cache_prefetch=false to reduce mem pressure.
5) Create an incident ticket and attach triage artifacts (traces, kernel histograms, prompt sample cases).

Guidance for kernel scheduling experiments

- Sweep one scheduler knob at a time and keep a consistent baseline. Use the control-group-run pattern to reduce variance.
- Prefer deterministic synthetic co-tenants for repeatability (use our ri-sim synthetic driver).
- Measure fairness with the normalized-service-time metric (per-route weighted mean latency divided by baseline). Target fairness drift < 1.05 for production release.

Profiling playbook highlights

- Use combined sampling tracing (1% head, 100% compact traces for anomalies).
- Always collect kernel call stacks and kernel input size vectors for slow kernels. These vectors help map to particular attention heads and sequence lengths.
- Post-synthesis: generate an artifact bundle that includes: compact_trace.pbz, kernel_histogram.csv, fidelity-failcases.ndjson, nvml-snapshot.json. Name format: rdbundle-<date>-<runid>.

Benchmark hardening patterns (examples we've found effective)

- Noise-averaged baseline: run the same benchmark 5 times across random node placements and report mean + 95% CI to avoid single-node outliers.
- Shadow-run verification: run candidate kernel variant in shadow for 4 hours under production-sim and compare outputs; only switch on rollouts when shadow delta < fidelity SLO.
- Thermal stabilization window: after a kernel rollout, enforce a 12-hour stabilization window on a representative pool to capture thermal/driver regressions before global rollout.

Known-issue catalog (shortlist)

- KV cache fragmentation under repeated prefetch toggles (symptom: growing mem usage over 8+ hours). Mitigation: trigger cache compaction routine (ri-runtime kv-compact --slot <id>).
- Interleaved-batch mem-safety edge when slot coalescing > 6 (symptom: rare OOMs at peak). Mitigation: limit coalesce to 4 and enable guarded-allocation.
- Occasional nvlink ECC counters increment after multi-hour soak on specific A100 hosts (symptom: msgs in host logs). Mitigation: route traffic away from host and open hardware escalation.

Release gate checklist

1) Microbenchmark sweep: pass.
2) Scheduler perturbation: no fairness drift > 1.05 and no P999 jumps > 2x baseline.
3) Fidelity replay: golden corpus delta < 2% and critical prompt failcases documented.
4) Production soak: no kernel watchdog restarts; <1 incident per 24h for the run.
5) Artifact bundle uploaded and linked to release note.

Operational ownership and escalation

- Primary oncall: serving-runtime team (pager duty rota).
- Secondary: infra-sre for host/GPU hardware issues.
- Escalation criteria: persistent P99 regressions after rollback attempts or hardware error counters increment.

Appendix: artifact naming and retention

- Artifact naming: rdbundle-<team>-<suite>-YYYYMMDD-HHMM-<runid>. Example: rdbundle-runtime-fidelity-20260201-0300-4f2c.
- Retention policy: keep artifact bundles for 90 days on S3; critical incident bundles (severity P1/P2) archived for 2 years.

Contacts and acknowledgements

- Document owner: Aisha Patel (runtime reliability)
- Reviewers: Diego Martinez (profiling), Rina Kaur (benchmarks)
- Related owners: Kernel team, Scheduler team, Observability team

This manual is intended to be used by engineers preparing releases, oncall responders, and performance engineers who own benchmark fidelity and stability. If it is useful, we will convert the frequent triage steps into a small automation suite (ri-auto-hardening) to reduce manual sweep errors.
